records.author: armstrongb
records.storyText:
Hi, I built acceptodds, a prediction market on conference peer review. Every ICLR 2027 submission (42k papers) has a market: Accept vs. Reject.

Like many in the ML community, I think the current conference/paper situation is a bit broken. I'm not sure how to fix it, but this is my attempt at building something fun to get the conversation started.

Some details: - Prices come from Hanson's LMSR (logarithmic market scoring rule).

- You can sell and/or rebuy at any time

- There's a public leaderboard that ranks traders by P&L.

- It uses an in-app currency called reputation. It can't be converted to money.

- Bots can trade too, and they're encouraged. If you can get an LLM to predict the market, that would be cool! There's a public HTTP API with an OpenAPI spec (/api/v1/openapi.json).

- Comments are pseudonymous, like on OpenReview ("User k3xm"), but they show the author's position.

- There's also a 2D map of all submissions: https://acceptodds.com/map

How would you extend this? How should ML conference reviews work? Is there something better than open review?

Go find your own paper (if you have one), place a bet and LMK what you think :)

records.title: Show HN: Meanwhile Map – what else was happening in the world at the same time
records.author: 29b
records.storyText:
When reading a history book, I sometimes have a hard time internalizing when the events are taking place. Sure, I know the dates, but it takes a bit of effort to put them in a broader context, to understand where in history they belong. What usually helps is to put them in relation to other contemporaneous events. To play around with this, I've made Meanwhile Map. You select a date and a time window, then scroll around the world map to see a list of contemporaneous events. For example, yes, the Mughal Empire was founded by Babur in the 1520s, but it paints a different picture in my head when I see that this roughly coincides with Cortés' capture of Tenochtitlan, or that it's close to the Siege of Vienna. Example link: https://meanwhilemap.com/#y=1520&m=1&span=120&off=founded,pe...

On the technical side, the app is a single static web page. It uses Wikidata for data (via SPARQL) and OpenHistoricalMap to show the events on the political map of the time. It's open source (https://github.com/ea/meanwhilemap/tree/main), vibe coded as an experiment. All processing is client-side, and no data is tracked other than simple visitor counts.

records.title: Show HN: Tofu – let your agent deploy full-stack apps
records.storyText:
Hi HN,

I'm the founder of Tofu, a code deployment platform built for agents. Paste our setup prompt to any agent you're already using and Tofu enables your agent to take your project from code to production. Current features include frontend & backend hosting (created & managed by Tofu), Postgres database (created & managed by Tofu), domain management (one-click setup for Cloudflare managed domains, manual DNS record for others), authentication, Google login, and Analytics.

We built Tofu out of our personal frustrations: we're engineers who know how to code, we've deployed live products and understand the process, and our AI agents have already finished writing the code that works locally, yet taking a product fully online still took 2-3 hours: - Setup hosting, backend, database - Copy-pasting a lot of apikeys/secrets from here to there - Setting up correct redirect urls from places to places - Managing DNS records, domains - Setting up a lot services (email, 3rd parth OAuth, etc) - Payments

Tofu works with any MCP-compatible agents, and here's a list of tested agents (10+ different projects end-to-end deployment via Tofu): local coding agents (Claude Code, Codex/ChatGPT, Kimi Code, DSH, Cursor), Instinct, Muse, Kimi Code cloud.

None of that is hard, but each of these services have their own providers and it involves managing 5-10 different accounts. Most cloud providers have their own CLI, but it only works within their own platform and the process still involves a lot of manual interventions. Agents can call any API and use CLIs, but cannot open a Google Cloud project or put a card on file with 5 vendors.

We think deployment is not a compute problem, but an accounts problem. Our endgoal is to utilize SSO across services, and provide agents the ability to deploy a live product end-to-end. We don't want to compete with any cloud providers, but to make agents actually capable of shipping "live" products. We're rolling out features to support buy domains directly from Tofu (we're an authorized reseller of Name.com), and provide more customizability to tech stacks.

We're still very early and have just launched our product, please send us any feedbacks, comments, and we promise we will respond to every single one of them.

records.title: Show HN: Self-bench – benchmark coding agents on real-world software
records.author: avyayv
records.storyText:
Hey HN,

Today, we're launching selfbench.dev, an open-source tool that lets you create and run evals automatically from your PRs.

Every benchmark with sufficient trust eventually gets benchmaxxed (Goodhart's law) - the labs are incentivized to maximize their scores on that benchmark, which isn't predictive on whether it'll actually work within your setup. This has been a time-consuming process that only the largest companies can afford to do, so we built self-bench to fix this.

Self-bench uses agents to author / review Harbor environments generated from your PRs. You then approve every eval that the agent created, and can model/harness evals concurrently on sandboxes.

To save you money, we also allow you to connect your OpenAI and Claude subscriptions so you don't have to pay raw token costs.

We ran evals on several large codebases like

- Posthog (https://selfbench.dev/PostHog/posthog)

- Next.js (https://selfbench.dev/vercel/next.js)

- Sentry (https://selfbench.dev/getsentry/sentry)

- Pi (https://selfbench.dev/earendil-works/pi)

- as well as other fantastic open-source projects (all on selfbench.dev)

From our evals:

- Kimi K3 and GLM 5.3 are almost always more expensive, yet less performant than models like GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5, due to token efficiency.

- GPT-6 Luna is almost always the most effective "cost-efficient" model we've tested, not open-source models.

We'd love for you to try this on your codebase and let us know what you think!

records.title: Show HN: A replacement motherboard for the iPod mini, 3G and 4G
records.author: seanpod
records.storyText:
I’ve always wanted to get on the dedicated music train, but I can’t get over no wireless headphones and no streaming. So I made a drop-in replacement motherboard for the iPod mini, 3rd and 4th generation iPod.

I’ve reverse engineered the original LCD, so it keeps the original display and click wheel. Externally the iPod is unchanged, apart from a USB-C port.

Inside, there’s Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, a Raspberry Pi Compute Module Zero, an RP2350, and a CS43131 DAC. The Pi runs Linux, so Spotify and Apple Music work, but it’s also just a small Linux computer so you can run whatever you want on it.

There are two versions: Pi and Pico.

Sprout Pico is built around the RP2350 and is focused on local playback. It gives your iPod Bluetooth and WiFi. This is the only board the iPod mini supports.

Sprout Pi adds the CM0 on top of that. The RP2350 still owns the hardware and can run independently, and the CM0 adds Linux for things like Spotify and Apple Music. So when you’re just listening to local music, the Pi doesn’t need to be running at all. The aim is to keep the flexibility of Linux for streaming while maximising battery life for offline listening. This dual processor split is still a work in progress but planned for the next revision.

Would love to get your thoughts, and any features you’d like to see!

records.title: Show HN: Paganel – Data migration with a receipt you can verify later
records.author: stan_stork
records.storyText:
Paganel comes from an old work problem: I had a large schema migration with lots of transformations and several environments to check. One of the main requirements was to validate whether the data had moved correctly, and I was not allowed to use any SaaS tools because it was forbidden for data to leave our network. Since I couldn't find any air-gapped tool that could do both the transformation and the verification (basic row counts aren't enough for transformed data), I had to write custom scripts for the entire process.

Ever since then, the idea of automating complex migrations has stuck in my head, which led me to start building Paganel a year and a half ago.

In Paganel, a migration is just a single declarative file. You specify where the data comes from and where it's going, and the rest goes in the same file: joins, filters, computed fields, and validation rules.

If you are missing a specific source, sink, transform, or filter, you can easily extend Paganel by writing your own WASM plugin in Rust or JS. These execute inside a strict sandbox, so they don't have any filesystem or network access unless you allow it in the migration config.

I also wanted to make large migrations simple, so before running a real migration, you can run pag plan to review the output schema, the DDL, and the time and memory estimates. You can also use the plan to see a sample of real rows. They get processed through the whole pipeline, which gives you absolute clarity on what will actually be inserted.

One of the biggest challenges isn't just doing the migration, but verifying that everything actually moved correctly. For that, there is the --integrity flag. Pass it, and Paganel hashes the rows on the fly as they migrate, storing those hashes on disk, keyed by primary key. After the run, it uses them to spit out a 32-byte root hash for the table. Together with the row hashes, this gives you a complete 'migration receipt.'

Minutes or weeks later, you can run pag verify, and it re-reads the destination, recomputes the hashes and compares them with the receipt, without connecting to the source. When the root doesn't match, you know something changed, and then verify goes through the row hashes and tells you which rows it was.

It tells you that the destination still contains what Paganel wrote, but it can't tell you whether the transformation itself was correct.

Another huge factor is migration speed. I created a small benchmark to measure Paganel's speed and tested it on a 100M-row migration from MySQL to PostgreSQL (with the databases on separate servers). With the default config, which is a single stream, I got about 390k rows a second. Splitting the table into four parallel streams got it to almost 940k. The number of streams is configurable for tables with an integer primary key. Enabling the --integrity flag does add some overhead, dropping those numbers to 340k and 670k, respectively.

Paganel is still pre-v1.0, so there are some rough edges to be aware of:

- No CDC yet: Currently, it only handles batch processing. Continuous sync with verification is the ultimate goal, but nailing the batch engine comes first.

- Limited databases: Right now, Paganel only natively supports MySQL and PostgreSQL.

- API changes: The project is under heavy development, meaning the config syntax might change slightly from release to release.

- One-man team: I'm developing this solo. You will likely run into edge cases I haven't caught yet.

- Platform testing: The full integration suite and all my own manual testing run on Linux. macOS and Windows get pre-built binaries too, but they only go through a basic smoke test.

If you want to try it out, the quickstart in the README will spin up some sample databases in Docker for you.

How do you verify migrations today? I'd like to know whether a receipt like this would fit into how you work.

records.storyText:
I have been working on Rashomon, an open-source execution recorder for AI coding agents.

The basic idea is that the agent transcript is not ground truth. Rashomon keeps its own record of what happened and compares it against the agent’s account.

For Claude Code, it records things like:

* shell commands, exit codes, and whether they may have written files * tool calls and outcomes * test commands and their outcomes * subagent lifecycle and ordering * timestamps and parent/child relationships * keyed digests of command/tool inputs and working directories

It builds a timeline from these events. It does not store prompts, responses, file contents, or tool output.

For example, it now detects patterns like:

`test fails → only test files change → same test passes`

and:

`test command fails → same command passes → no corresponding file edit`

These can indicate that an agent changed a test instead of fixing the underlying issue.

Rashomon currently runs as a Claude Code plugin or through the CLI.

CLI:

`rashomon watch`

then:

`rashomon report`

Plugin:

`/rashomon:report`

There are still edge cases around cwd, git state, test-selection arguments, generated files, retries, and parallel execution. I would be interested in feedback from people building agents on what execution signals you would want Rashomon to capture or correlate.

GitHub: https://github.com/altrace-dev-role/rashomon

records.author: schoenobates

Hey all - I made a thing with my clanker Kevin: Ototo (https://ototo.dev/) - yes this is clanker driven dev. The idea is to offload code exploration and other token'y heavy tasks to a smaller model to do the work and chuck the result back. This helps in a couple of ways (1) it saves tokens if you can offload to a cheaper or free local model (2) it can keep the main context clearer as it removes all the sherlocking thinking/exploration. It also saves more tokens than using anthropics own exploration agent.

I had originally played around with a graph based approach but found this to work better. Currently, I have this running with Qwen 3.8 27B on my framework (I had Kevin build me a custom inference engine to squeeze all the juice I could out of the AMD - https://gitlab.com/handmadedigital/projects/shocho).

It's been through a bunch of tests (results are available if people want) against a load of different repos, including comparing subsequent commits of large repos with claude, claude + exploration agent and claude + ototo and so far ototo seems to really help.

The site is very 'LLM'y at the moment - I haven't had time to edit it to make the text more readable for us humans. Sorry.

Hope it helps folks in their day-to-day.

records.title: Show HN: Aether: Check and fix web accessibility issues from your coding agent
records.author: samy_patra
records.storyText:
Hi, HackerNews!

I'm Samy, co-founder of Allchemy Labs. We built Aether, an MCP server that enables engineers to check for, understand, and fix web accessibility issues all from their IDE. Your preferred coding agent can leverage Aether to open a webpage, scan it using axe-core and return a short, prioritized list of violations along with code fixes or guidance. Every suggested fix is re-tested in a real browser before you see it, and once you apply it, your agent can re-scan the page to verify it worked. You never need to open a browser, use multiple tools, or be an expert in WCAG criteria.

Aether uses our own custom ontology architecture to provide grounded insights to any WCAG violations the scanner finds. Every WCAG technique the engine cites must pass our quality gate. Specifically, it must satisfy the violated success criterion, apply to that kind of element, and remediate that axe rule. If nothing passes, our engine will abstain rather than guess.

We compared Aether against standalone coding agent on its own (Opus 5, 30 anonymized live sites, 111 targets). While the results were mixed we have published the results especially calling out specific wins and improvement opportunities for our insight engine. Read the study here: https://allchemylabs.substack.com/p/we-tested-our-own-access...

Try Aether today, no signup needed. npx -y @allchemylabs/aether-wcag-scanner (any MCP client: Claude Code, Cursor, Codex…) Claude Code plugin: /plugin marketplace add https://github.com/allchemylabs/claude-plugins.git then /plugin install aether-wcag-scanner@allchemylabs Without a key you get the browser scan, local template fixes and verification. A free beta key adds the cloud engine: https://beta.allchemylabs.ai/?src=hn

Feedback from people who have used accessibility scanners and/or suggestion engines would be highly valuable to us, as we aim to build a tool that solves real problems and makes people's lives easier.

Happy to answer any questions and hope to hear from you.

Note: Right now Aether only checks WCAG 2.1 AA. Sites behind bot protection (e.g. Cloudflare challenges) return a "blocked" result instead of a fake scan, so point it at localhost or staging.

records.title: Show HN: Lask – A task runner with a type system and pinned Docker environments
records.author: torudev
records.storyText:
I implemented a task runner called Lask. Let me introduce it to you.

Lask is a lightweight task runner with a statically typed DSL. It runs by calling Docker from Lask on the host.

Makefiles or shell scripts I wrote often failed to run on my colleagues' machines, and I lost count of how many times I had to debug them. YAML-based CI/CD pipelines often fail after waiting for a lot of minutes, which make me angry.

When I was looking for a tool to solve this problem, I found Dagger. Dagger seemed to good for me. Dagger runs pipelines on Docker, so it is highly portable and can use the type system of general-purpose languages.

However, Dagger was too much for me. Dagger does not run on its own, and requires to set up a general-purpose language ecosystem. I feel like I was using heavy machinery to move a potted plant. I want to call a tool with only a single binary and one file.

So I decided to create Lask. I want to call simple function with simple command. I want to fix the type and environment of the function.

command { "node", "npm", "npx" } on #node:20.20.2-alpine3.23 test() = $ npm test

$ lask run test

I made a tool that can extract errors immediately by type, run the same way on local and CI, and call simply. You can use Lask with a single binary of the lask command and Docker installed. Lask has LSP, so you can use completion and syntax highlighting. You can complete not only the lask command, but also the functions that lask calls. I considered practical use, so it can be called declared commands, such as `lask cmd psql ...` to check data manually, or `lask cmd kubectl get pods`.

However, Lask does not have as many as Dagger's features, cannot use the advanced ecosystem of general-purpose languages. Also, Lask is not a build system, so it does not optimize builds by detecting differences. Lask is just a tool to call builder tools.

Lask is licensed under MIT, currently at version 0.7.0 before official release. The implementation is in Haskell. It distributes binaries for Linux/Windows/MacOS.

Any feedback is welcome. I would be happy to receive comments. More detailed specifications and more practical examples are described in the README. Please take a look. Thank you for reading to the end. Please forgive my poor English.

records.storyText:
Hey HN!

We built SendOps because we think email can be a good medium to help users through their journey with your product. Onboarding a new user and helping them in their journey in your product can be specific to the actions they take, their goals and it allows them to read or explore in their own time and not based on your timeline.

After a while of running a service for a few years, we all end up with a few thousand if not hundreds of thousands of emails who signed up for our service. Some become customers, some never try the service and some might activate at some point in the future, when the time is right.

Email workflows (drip campaigns etc) have existed for a long time. However, all workflow providers charge both per email and per contact you have on your books. This usually means one of two things:

1. you pay a lot of money for contacts you don't email often. 2. you have to keep modifying your list based on your communication to avoid higher bills.

We also wanted to be able to build effective and useful email workflows using our coding agents. The result of our work is SendOps: SendOps is an email workflow product that sends emails through your own AWS SES account, charges no fees for contacts, or per email (just a flat fee subscription) and lets your coding agents help you with building your email workflows.

We hope you find SendOps useful. We've been members of HN community for a long time and love how direct and helpful your feedback is. So, please try it out if you think it can be useful to you (we have free-forever tier) and let us know what you think!

https://sendops.dev

Thank you

records.storyText:
Hey HN! Sharing this script I've been using professionally and personally to stop the crazy influx of cold emails that I get daily.

It works in the following way:

1. Copy + install the Google Apps script in your Gmail. The script runs every 10 minutes by default.

2. The script will automatically use a series of Regexes as a first line of defense (modify as you like!). If that fails it will use an LLM of your choice to make the call (this is optional but highly effective).

3. Flagged emails skip the inbox and get tagged with a "Cold email" label. Nothing gets deleted.

From running this for the past couple of weeks, it catches 99% of all cold emails and helps me stay in flow state. Hope this helps other people too!

records.title: Show HN: Open-Source Instinct
records.author: mariagorskikh
records.storyText:
We’ve all heard that Instinct raised $1 billion to bring personal AI agents to everyone.

But I think anyone can build their own Instinct for a specific group of people. You know your audience, understand what they need, and know how to reach them.

So I built an open-source version.

It can make purchases online, coordinate with other people’s agents, use a computer, connect to MCP tools, manage permissions + everything else instinct wants to do.

Here’s the stack:

- Pi, the open-source agent framework used by openclaw - Maritime for each agent’s VM and computer access (cheapest infra) - Composio for app integrations and managed Google OAuth - Inkbox for imessege + email

If you want to start selling your own personal AI agent, you can host the backend on a platform like railway/vercel (around $20 a month). Maritime handles provisioning each agent’s VM and the infrastructure behind it ($1 a month per agent)

I’m open-sourcing this so we can build on it together: add more services and tools, better permissions, different payment strategies, better prompts...

The goal is to make it easy and affordable for anyone to launch a startup selling agents so that the world isnt ruled by openai dots and meta muses

Check it out and let me know what you think!
